title: Ask a hospital's model about several plans

blocks.text: A hospital plans its equipment renewals with a small model, and its engineers want unit tests of the form "this plan must be allowed, that one refused". They need one helper first: `verdicts(model, x, plans)`, which says, for each plan in a list, whether the model accepts it.
The model the tests build, for projects $`i`$ with start windows $`T_i`$ and a cost $`c_i`$ paid in the start year:
$`o_t`$ is overtime spending, which the hospital may use when a year runs over. It has no objective; any plan that meets the rows is acceptable.

Write `verdicts(model, x, plans)`. `x` maps each `(project, year)` to its start variable, and each plan maps each started project to its start year; every project not in a plan is not started. Return one answer per plan, in order: `True` when the model accepts exactly that plan, `False` when it refuses it. A plan that starts a project in a year the project has no variable for is refused. Solve with HiGHS through MathOpt.

The engineers share one model between many questions, and a planner may already have fixed a start by its bounds (an override). While a plan is being asked, the plan alone decides every start: fix each start variable to 1 or 0 as the plan says, replacing whatever bounds it had, an override's included. When `verdicts` returns, put the bounds back, so every start variable has the bounds it had when the function was called. About twelve lines.

"""Run executes this file. Change the calls and see what prints. Submit grades."""
import logging

# Turn the logger up, so the `log.debug` lines of your code show under the printed lines.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

from ortools.math_opt.python import mathopt

from verdict import verdicts

# A school's projects: start years allowed and cost in the start year ($k); 60 per year.
windows = {"roof": (2031, 2032), "gym": (2031,), "boiler": (2032,)}
cost = {"roof": 45, "gym": 30, "boiler": 25}
model = mathopt.Model()
x = {(n, t): model.add_binary_variable(name=f"x_{n}_{t}") for n, years in windows.items() for t in years}
for n, years in windows.items():
    model.add_linear_constraint(sum(x[n, t] for t in years) <= 1, name=f"once_{n}")
for t in (2031, 2032):
    model.add_linear_constraint(sum(cost[n] * x[n, t] for n in windows if t in windows[n]) <= 60, name=f"budget_{t}")
x["roof", 2032].lower_bound = 1.0

plans = [{"roof": 2032, "gym": 2031}, {"roof": 2031, "gym": 2031}, {"roof": 2032, "boiler": 2032},
         {"roof": 2032, "gym": 2033}]
for plan, ok in zip(plans, verdicts(model, x, plans)):
    print(f"plan {plan}:", ok)
print("roof 2032 bounds afterwards:", (x["roof", 2032].lower_bound, x["roof", 2032].upper_bound))

from __future__ import annotations

from ortools.math_opt.python import mathopt


def verdicts(model: mathopt.Model, x: dict[tuple[str, int], mathopt.Variable], plans: list[dict[str, int]]) -> list[bool]:
    """For each plan (project -> start year), does `model` accept it? Every bound is left as found."""
    # TODO: fix each plan into the model, solve, read the answer, and leave the model as found.
    return [True for plan in plans]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = mathopt.Model()
    x = {("boiler", 2027): model.add_binary_variable(name="x_boiler_2027")}
    model.add_linear_constraint(x["boiler", 2027] == 1, name="must_boiler")
    print(verdicts(model, x, [{"boiler": 2027}, {}]))

cases.says: a plan whose yearly cost fits the budget is allowed, and one that needs more than budget and overtime together is refused
a plan that leaves out the must-do is refused, because nothing the plan does not start may be started for it
a plan that fits only with overtime is allowed, because overtime is not a start decision
a plan that starts a project in a year it has no variable for is refused, not read as some other plan
a start already fixed by a planner's override keeps its bounds afterwards, not the 0-to-1 bounds of an unfixed start

origin.section: Fix the Plan, Then Ask the Solver: Allowed or Refused

concepts: a unit test fixes every start decision by its bounds, leaves helper variables free, and reads the termination reason
